classification.difficultyReason: Factorises quadratic trigonometric equations, rejects an impossible ratio and handles reciprocal denominators before finding all restricted-domain solutions.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2\sin^2\theta-3\sin\theta+1&=0\\(2\sin\theta-1)(\sin\theta-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$ or $\sin\theta=1$.

For $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$, $A=\sin^{-1}(\tfrac12)=30^\circ$. Sine is positive in Q1 and Q2, so $\theta=30^\circ$ or $180^\circ-30^\circ=150^\circ$.

For $\sin\theta=1$, $\theta=90^\circ$.

Thus $\theta=30^\circ,90^\circ,150^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-3&=0\\(2\cos\theta-3)(\cos\theta+1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\cos\theta=\tfrac32$ or $\cos\theta=-1$.

Since $-1\le\cos\theta\le1$, $\cos\theta=\tfrac32$ has no solution.

For $\cos\theta=-1$, $\theta=180^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta&=0\\\cos\theta(2\cos\theta-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\cos\theta=0$ or $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$.

For $\cos\theta=0$, $\theta=90^\circ$ or $270^\circ$.

For $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, $A=\cos^{-1}(\tfrac12)=60^\circ$. Cosine is positive in Q1 and Q4, so $\theta=60^\circ$ or $360^\circ-60^\circ=300^\circ$.

Thus $\theta=60^\circ,90^\circ,270^\circ,300^\circ$.

The denominators require $\cos\theta\ne0$. Multiplying by $\cos^2\theta$ gives
$$\begin{align*}1+\cos\theta-2\cos^2\theta&=0\\2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-1&=0\\(2\cos\theta+1)(\cos\theta-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\cos\theta=-\tfrac12$ or $\cos\theta=1$.

For $\cos\theta=-\tfrac12$, $A=\cos^{-1}(\tfrac12)=60^\circ$. Cosine is negative in Q2 and Q3, giving $\theta=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$ or $180^\circ+60^\circ=240^\circ$.

For $\cos\theta=1$, $\theta=0^\circ$ in the stated domain. The endpoint $360^\circ$ is excluded.

Thus $\theta=0^\circ,120^\circ,240^\circ$.
